name: Torsemide

lead: Torsemide is a loop diuretic, a strong water pill, that people in depuffing circles mention as a way to get a leaner, more defined face by shedding retained fluid.

It works by reducing sodium reabsorption in the kidney, so more salt and water leave in the urine and less fluid sits in the tissues. It is prescribed for fluid buildup from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease; it has about 80-90% oral bioavailability and a longer effect than furosemide. The large TRANSFORM-HF trial compared it with furosemide in heart failure, and no published study has tested it on facial puffiness.

paras: It is a prescription tablet, and in medicine it is taken on a schedule set by a doctor for fluid overload. In appearance discussions it is described as a short-term way to look drier and more defined, and the effect shows up as increased urination within hours of a dose.

Reported effects include headache, frequent urination, diarrhea, cough and dizziness; low potassium and hearing loss are less common, and dehydration and electrolyte loss are the main concern. It is not advised in pregnancy or breastfeeding and is prescription-only.

angle.text: Torsemide is discussed in depuffing circles as a strong water pill for a leaner, more defined face. It clears retained water through the kidneys, which is the step people expect to translate into less facial puffiness. It is prescribed for heart-failure fluid overload and has not been studied for appearance.

lead: Torsemide, also spelled torasemide, is a loop diuretic and sulfonamide used mainly to relieve fluid accumulation from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease. It can be given orally or intravenously and is sold under names such as Demadex.[1][2]

It was patented in 1974 and entered medical use in 1993, and it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1] Trials have compared it with furosemide in heart failure; the large TRANSFORM-HF trial reported no significant difference in all-cause mortality between the two.[3]
No published research has examined torsemide for cosmetic purposes such as facial depuffing.

paras: Torsemide is used to treat fluid overload in heart failure and is sometimes used for high blood pressure, although it is a less preferred option there.[1] The US label lists edema associated with heart failure, renal disease and hepatic disease, and hypertension.[2]

A 2001 open-label randomised trial compared torsemide with furosemide in heart failure patients.[4] The pragmatic TRANSFORM-HF randomised trial, which enrolled nearly 3,000 patients after a heart-failure hospitalisation, reported no significant difference in all-cause mortality between torsemide and furosemide.[3] Wikipedia describes earlier and smaller analyses as linking torsemide to fewer rehospitalisations.[1]

Headache, frequent urination, diarrhea, cough and dizziness are described as common, while hearing loss and low potassium are less common. Wikipedia states that no evidence shows torsemide causes ototoxicity in humans, and notes that loop diuretics may deplete thiamine with long-term use.[1]

Torsemide reduces sodium reabsorption in the kidney. Oral bioavailability is roughly 80-90%, protein binding exceeds 99%, and about 80% is metabolised in the liver; a pharmacokinetic comparison in heart-failure patients found differences from furosemide in absorption and effect.[1][5]

Torsemide is prescription-only. It is listed among loop diuretics discussed as gray-market water pills in looksmaxxing contexts; the sources reviewed contain no substantive community discussion of it. In May 2024 the US FDA conditionally approved a torsemide solution for dogs with heart failure.[1]
No studies found on torsemide for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Trials in heart failure include TRANSFORM-HF and an open-label comparison with furosemide.[3][4]
